title: Accessible Medical Translation for Low Vision Patients
summary: Build accessible medical translation workflows with large print, screen-reader text, audio, and teach-back for patients with low vision.
body_markdown:
###


A U.S. clinic should record the patient’s preferred spoken language, preferred written language, relevant dialect, usable document format, and assistive technology needs as separate fields. Confirm these preferences at the encounter because language preference does not reveal whether the patient uses large print, a screen reader, audio, or Braille.


###


No. Spoken interpretation supports a live conversation, while written translation converts text between languages, and accessibility determines whether the patient can use the resulting document. A U.S. care team should address each need when discharge instructions, medication directions, or consent materials must remain usable after the visit.


###


A clinic should offer the format the patient can use, which may include large print, accessible digital text, preferred-language audio, or Braille when requested. In a U.S. clinical workflow, staff should test the final material with the patient’s device or reading method instead of assuming one format works for every person with low vision.


###


No. Opalite Health can support healthcare-specific spoken interpretation across 150+ languages and dialects and medical document translation, but the care organization remains responsible for producing and testing usable formats such as large print, Braille, and screen-reader-ready files. This distinction applies to U.S. clinical and patient-education workflows.


###


The care team should check both understanding and independent access before discharge. In the patient’s preferred language, ask the patient to explain the plan in their own words, then confirm that they can open, read, hear, or otherwise retrieve the translated instructions using the format and device they will have at home.
